description: Cross-driver repeat-key vectors (PAR-2): the magic key typed after a character that no hotstring claimed doubles that character, but only mid-word. Replayed by the Windows engine (HSE_TryRepeatKey), the macOS expander (try_repeat_feature) and the Linux rule (repeat_key.resolve). Only cases on which the three drivers agree belong here.

field_semantics.buffer: The typed buffer INCLUDING the magic key just typed, which is the last character of the buffer. The buffer starts at a word boundary unless start_is_word_boundary says otherwise.
field_semantics.start_is_word_boundary: Optional, true when absent: whether the buffer's own start abuts a word boundary. When false the buffer's first character may be the middle of an older word.
field_semantics.word_character: One rule on the three drivers, _shared/lua/text_utils is_hotstring_word_char: every non-ASCII character, @, letters, digits and underscore are word characters; a space, newline, punctuation, quote, parenthesis or hyphen is not.
field_semantics.replacement: When it fires: the character that is doubled, so the buffer afterwards is the buffer without the magic key plus this character.

vectors.description: A letter after another letter doubles: po then the key gives poo.
A two-byte or two-code-unit-wide letter is doubled whole, never by its trailing byte.
The rule applies in a later word of the buffer, not only the first.
The first letter of the buffer is a word start: c then the key must not give cc (the user wants a text expansion there).
The first letter of a later word is a word start too.
A newline opens a word as a space does.
A period before the letter makes it a word start.
After an opening quote the letter is the first of its word.
A space before the key is never repeated.
A newline before the key is never repeated.
The key as the whole buffer has no character before it.
A digit is a word character: the letter after it is not a word start.
An underscore is a word character.
A parenthesis is not a word character: the letter after it is the first of its word.
A hyphen is not a word character.
The key repeating itself is a second trigger, never doubled.
When the buffer's start is not a known word boundary its first character may be the tail of an older word, so a repeat resting on it is refused.
With a third character the repeat does not rest on the buffer's first one.
The key is read from the caller, so a user who changed it gets the same behaviour.
